title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 77–78
description: Curated fixed-order binomials, initialisms, spoken acronyms, clippings and written abbreviations with original examples and Brazilian Portuguese translations.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow the teaching topics and relevant exercise vocabulary; examples and notes are newly written. Original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Checked study sections, register and pronunciation notes, exercises 77.1–77.4 and 78.1–78.5, and the corresponding answer key.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA where confidently transcribed; full initialisms use a letter-by-letter speechText target. Longer idiomatic phrases omit unverified IPA rather than supplying guesses.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared entries with all relevant source teaching pages and answer-key entries; verified lexical meaning, register, word order, unique IDs, schema and conservative word-audio targeting.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio or live VocabLab browser import, browser TTS or speech-recognition test was performed.

units.title: Unit 77 — Binomials
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 77. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise fixed pairs linked by and, or, but and to, and preserve their conventional word order.
Distinguish literal and idiomatic meanings of frequent binomials in speech and writing.
Use near-synonym pairs and grammatical-word binomials with natural collocations and register.
Apply exercise-based contrasts, including back and forth, black and white and ladies and gentlemen.

sectionsChecked: C: Binomials composed of grammar words
D: Binomials linked by words other than and

items.section: A · Fixed binomials and sound patterns
items.example: We have finished the main installation, but there are still a few odds and ends to sort out.
items.note: Fixed order: odds and ends, not ends and odds; often means small remaining tasks or objects.

items.section: A · Fixed binomials and sound patterns
items.example: Successful teamwork requires give and take from everyone.
items.note: The noun phrase means mutual compromise, not physically giving and taking objects.

items.section: A · Fixed binomials and sound patterns
items.example: Unexpected delays are part and parcel of developing new hardware.
items.note: Usually part and parcel of something; means an unavoidable or essential element.

items.section: A · Fixed binomials and sound patterns
items.example: He started to rant and rave when the flight was cancelled.
items.note: A verb pair for speaking angrily and loudly; both verbs can change tense together.

items.section: A · Fixed binomials and sound patterns
items.example: Without regular repairs, the abandoned house went to rack and ruin.
items.note: Normally in the expression go to rack and ruin; describes severe neglect or decay.

items.pt: excessivamente formal e correto; muito recatado
items.section: A · Fixed binomials and sound patterns
items.example: The interviewer seemed prim and proper, but was actually very friendly.
items.note: Describes someone who behaves very formally and cares greatly about propriety.

items.section: A · Fixed binomials and sound patterns
items.example: Our first prototype was rough and ready, but it demonstrated the basic principle.
items.note: Often informal; simple, imperfect or not highly polished, but potentially effective.

items.pt: levar para jantar e oferecer boa comida e bebida; recepcionar com requinte
items.section: A · Fixed binomials and sound patterns
items.example: The company planned to wine and dine its international visitors after the conference.
items.note: Verb expression for entertaining someone, especially at restaurants; it does not require drinking wine.

items.section: A · Fixed binomials and sound patterns
items.example: The cancelled train left dozens of passengers high and dry.
items.note: Usually leave someone high and dry, without the help or resources they need.

items.section: B · Similar-meaning pairs
items.example: With so few available components, we cannot afford to pick and choose.
items.note: Means having the freedom to select only the things you prefer.

items.section: B · Similar-meaning pairs
items.example: Her confidence in technical presentations has grown in leaps and bounds.
items.note: Usually grow, develop, improve or progress in leaps and bounds; by leaps and bounds is also used.

items.section: B · Similar-meaning pairs
items.example: After the noisy workshop, all I wanted was some peace and quiet.
items.note: A calm environment without disturbance; often used with some or a bit of.

items.section: B · Similar-meaning pairs
items.example: The team took a few days off for some rest and recreation after the deadline.
items.note: Sometimes abbreviated R and R; recreation means enjoyable relaxation or activities.

items.pt: acima de tudo; em primeiro lugar
items.section: B · Similar-meaning pairs
items.example: First and foremost, we must ensure the new system is safe to operate.
items.note: Introduces the most important point, ahead of secondary considerations.

items.pt: aqui e ali; em alguns lugares
items.section: C · Binomials built from grammar words
items.example: We found small scratches here and there on the equipment casing.
items.note: Means in scattered places, not everywhere.

items.section: C · Binomials built from grammar words
items.example: We have been discussing the proposal on and off for several months.
items.note: Alternates between happening and stopping; off and on is a valid reversed variant.

items.pt: de um lado para o outro; para lá e para cá
items.section: C · Binomials built from grammar words
items.example: The two departments sent the design files back and forth all morning.
items.note: Describes repeated movement or exchange in opposite directions; do not reverse to forth and back.

items.pt: para lá e para cá; de um lado para outro
items.section: C · Binomials built from grammar words
items.example: Technicians walked to and fro between the laboratory and the control room.
items.note: More literary or formal than back and forth; fixed order.

items.pt: ativo e saindo de casa; circulando
items.section: C · Binomials built from grammar words
items.example: After a week at home, she was out and about again.
items.note: Often describes resuming normal activities or going out after an illness.

items.pt: para cima e para baixo; de um lado para outro
items.section: C · Binomials built from grammar words
items.example: We went up and down the stairs looking for the missing keys.
items.note: Movement in both vertical directions; also figuratively repeated movement along a street.

items.section: C · Binomials built from grammar words
items.example: The archive contains several black and white photographs of the original laboratory.
items.note: Fixed order for pictures without colour; black-and-white is also common before a noun.

items.section: C · Binomials built from grammar words
items.example: Ladies and gentlemen, the presentation will begin in five minutes.
items.note: Conventional fixed-order formal address to an audience.

items.pt: ao contrário; com a frente virada para trás
items.section: D · Binomials with other linking words
items.example: He put his jumper on back to front without noticing.
items.note: Often used of clothes worn with the front and back reversed; not front to back in this sense.

items.pt: vencer ou fracassar por conta própria; virar-se sozinho
items.section: D · Binomials with other linking words
items.example: With almost no training, the new recruits were left to sink or swim.
items.note: Means having to succeed or fail without much support.

items.pt: devagar, mas com constância; aos poucos e de forma segura
items.section: D · Binomials with other linking words
items.example: Slowly but surely, the team eliminated the faults in the controller.
items.note: Highlights steady progress despite a slow pace; fixed order.

items.section: D · Binomials with other linking words
items.example: Sooner or later, we will need to replace the ageing equipment.
items.note: Refers to something expected to happen at an unspecified future time; not later or sooner.

items.section: D · Binomials with other linking words
items.example: For them, the decision was all or nothing.
items.note: Used when only complete success or no result at all is accepted; all-or-nothing before a noun.

items.pt: é pegar ou largar; aceitar ou recusar sem negociar
items.section: D · Binomials with other linking words
items.example: The seller said the offer was final: take it or leave it.
items.note: Presents an offer as non-negotiable; often blunt or informal.

items.pt: mais ou menos; com margem de diferença
items.section: D · Binomials with other linking words
items.example: The journey should take two hours, give or take ten minutes.
items.note: Used after an estimate to allow a small difference above or below it.

units.title: Unit 78 — Abbreviations and acronyms
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 78. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish initialisms spoken as separate letters from acronyms pronounced as words.
Interpret institutional, everyday, technological and health-related abbreviations in context.
Recognise clipped informal words and differences in British and American usage.
Read common written abbreviations appropriately and choose natural spoken forms for audio practice.

sectionsChecked: A: Abbreviations pronounced as individual letters

items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: institutions
items.example: I heard an interview with the scientist on the BBC.
items.note: British Broadcasting Corporation; normally pronounced as separate letters, with final-letter stress.

items.pt: CIA; agência de inteligência dos Estados Unidos
items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: institutions
items.example: The article referred to an investigation involving the CIA.
items.note: Central Intelligence Agency; a US government intelligence organisation; letter-by-letter pronunciation.

items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: institutions
items.example: The new regulation applies to many companies in the EU.
items.note: European Union; pronounced as individual letters.

items.pt: FBI; polícia federal investigativa dos Estados Unidos
items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: institutions
items.example: The FBI released a statement about the investigation.
items.note: Federal Bureau of Investigation; pronounced as separate letters.

items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: institutions
items.example: The novel follows an MI6 officer working overseas.
items.note: The book expands it as Military Intelligence 6; pronounced as the letter names M and I, then six.

items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: institutions
items.example: The WHO has published guidance about vaccination programmes.
items.note: World Health Organisation in the book; spoken as letter names, not as the word who.

items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: everyday uses
items.example: Please bring some photo ID to the reception desk.
items.note: Short for identity; often identification papers or a card; read as I D.

items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: everyday uses
items.example: The supermarket sells products labelled as GM food.
items.note: Genetically modified; normally said as the letters G M.

items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: everyday uses
items.example: Researchers analysed DNA from the sample.
items.note: Deoxyribonucleic acid; a substance carrying genetic information; say each letter.

items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: everyday uses
items.example: Check the FAQ page before contacting technical support.
items.note: Frequently asked questions; the letter-by-letter reading is appropriate here, though other pronunciations exist.

items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: everyday uses
items.example: The musician, AKA the Midnight Traveller, performed last night.
items.note: Also known as; often written AKA or aka; pronounced as the individual letters.

items.pt: vale de dívida; reconhecimento informal de débito
items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: everyday uses
items.example: He left an IOU promising to return the borrowed money.
items.note: Represents I owe you; a note acknowledging money or something else owed; individual letters.

items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: everyday uses
items.example: I withdrew cash from the ATM outside the station.
items.note: Automated teller machine; say A T M rather than one word.

items.pt: o mais rápido possível; assim que possível
items.section: A · Abbreviations spoken as letters: everyday uses
items.example: Please send the revised drawing ASAP.
items.note: As soon as possible; often said as individual letters, particularly in this unit.

items.pt: OTAN; Organização do Tratado do Atlântico Norte
items.section: B · Acronyms pronounced as words
items.example: The report discussed NATO's role in the region.
items.note: North Atlantic Treaty Organisation; pronounced as a single word, unlike BBC.

items.pt: senha numérica pessoal; código de identificação pessoal
items.section: B · Acronyms pronounced as words
items.example: Never share your PIN with anyone.
items.note: The book gives Personal Identity Number; pronounced as the word pin.

items.section: B · Acronyms pronounced as words
items.example: The article explains how SAD can affect energy during the darker months.
items.note: Seasonal affective disorder; pronounced as the word sad in this unit.

items.pt: ausente sem autorização; desaparecido sem avisar
items.section: B · Acronyms pronounced as words
items.example: A soldier was reported AWOL after failing to return to the base.
items.note: Absent without leave; a word-like military acronym, also used figuratively.

items.section: B · Acronyms pronounced as words
items.example: A laser measures the distance to the target.
items.note: Originally an acronym, but now treated as an ordinary word and written in lowercase.

items.section: B · Acronyms pronounced as words
items.example: The aircraft was detected by radar.
items.note: Originally an acronym; a familiar lowercase word for radio-based detection.

items.pt: mergulho autônomo com cilindro; equipamento autônomo de mergulho
items.section: B · Acronyms pronounced as words
items.example: She bought new scuba equipment before her holiday.
items.note: An established lowercase acronym; commonly scuba diving or scuba equipment.

items.section: B · Acronyms pronounced as words
items.example: The crew used sonar to identify objects underwater.
items.note: An established lowercase acronym relating to sound-based detection.

items.section: C · Informal shortened words
items.example: We need a kilo of rice for the event.
items.note: Informal shortened form of kilogram; commonly used with amounts and food.

items.section: C · Informal shortened words
items.example: The application update is about one gig in size.
items.note: Here it means gigabyte; gig can also mean a musical performance in another context.

items.section: C · Informal shortened words
items.example: The air con stopped working during the heatwave.
items.note: Informal clipping of air conditioning; British conversational usage.

items.pt: navegador GPS; sistema de navegação por satélite
items.section: C · Informal shortened words
items.example: We used the satnav to find the conference centre.
items.note: Clipping of satellite navigation; particularly common in British English.

items.section: C · Informal shortened words
items.example: She hopes to study engineering at uni next year.
items.note: Informal British shortening of university.

items.section: C · Informal shortened words
items.example: I left my mobile charging in the kitchen.
items.note: Short for mobile phone in British English; cell or cell phone in US English.

items.section: C · Informal shortened words
items.example: Could you call me on my cell later?
items.note: Informal American English short form of cell phone.

items.section: C · Informal shortened words
items.example: The coach suggested eating more carbs before the race.
items.note: Informal shortened plural of carbohydrates; common in nutrition talk.

items.section: C · Informal shortened words
items.example: They both enjoy sci-fi films set in space.
items.note: Informal abbreviation of science fiction, usually written with a hyphen.

items.section: C · Informal shortened words
items.example: The lab installed high-tech sensors to improve accuracy.
items.note: Clipped from high technology; commonly an adjective, often hyphenated before a noun.

items.pt: favor virar a página; veja no verso
items.section: D · Abbreviations mainly used in writing
items.example: The form continued on the next page, marked PTO at the bottom.
items.note: Please turn over; written instruction directing readers to the other side of a sheet.

items.section: D · Abbreviations mainly used in writing
items.example: At the end of the email, she added a PS about the meeting time.
items.note: Post script in the book; an additional message after the main body of a letter.

items.pt: favor confirmar presença; responda, por favor
items.section: D · Abbreviations mainly used in writing
items.example: The invitation asked guests to RSVP by Friday.
items.note: From French Répondez s'il vous plaît; asks recipients to reply to an invitation.

items.section: D · Abbreviations mainly used in writing
items.example: The words RIP were engraved on the old gravestone.
items.note: Rest in peace; frequently found on gravestones and memorials.
